chapters: Why we throw good after bad

units.t: The Sunk Cost Trap.
Part one. Two ski trips, one weekend.
Here's a little dilemma to start with.
A few months ago, you paid $100 for a ski weekend.
Then you spotted a cheaper deal and booked a second ski weekend for $50.
You're fairly sure you'll enjoy the cheaper one more.
Better snow, better company, shorter drive.
Now you realise both trips are on the same weekend, and neither can be refunded.
You can only go on one.
Which do you choose?
The sensible answer is the one you'll enjoy more.
The money is gone either way.
Whatever you pick, you've spent $150, and nothing you do now will bring any of it back.
The only thing still in play is how good your weekend is going to be.
Yet when the psychologists Hal Arkes and Catherine Blumer put this exact dilemma to students in 1985, more than half of them chose the $100 trip.
In their version, the trips were to Michigan and Wisconsin, and the students were told they'd enjoy Wisconsin more.
They still picked the dearer trip they expected to like less.
Somehow, the bigger payment felt like it deserved to be used.
Arkes and Blumer then took the idea out of the questionnaire and into the real world.
At the ticket window of a university theatre company in Ohio, people buying season tickets were quietly split into three groups.
Some paid the full price of $15.
Others, chosen at random, got a surprise discount of either $2 or $7.
Then the researchers simply tracked who turned up to the plays.
Over the first half of the season, the people who had paid full price went to noticeably more shows than the people who'd been given a discount.
Same plays, same seats, same free evenings.
The only difference was how much they'd already handed over.
This is the sunk cost trap.
A sunk cost is money, time or effort that you've already spent and can't get back.
The trap is letting that spent amount steer your next decision, when really only the future costs and benefits should count.
It's why people sit through a dreadful film because they paid for the ticket.
It's why we finish a meal we don't want because it wasn't cheap.
And it's why a car that keeps breaking down can feel impossible to sell, because you've just put new tyres on it.
The trap also has a famous nickname.
It's sometimes called the Concorde fallacy, after the supersonic passenger jet developed by the British and French governments.
Costs ballooned through the 1960s and 1970s, and it became clear the plane was very unlikely ever to earn back what had been spent.
Work carried on anyway, partly because so much had already gone in.
Concorde was a technical marvel, but only fourteen ever flew with airlines.
In the next part, we'll look at why our minds cling to spent money so stubbornly.
Part two. Why we throw good after bad.
There isn't just one reason we fall for sunk costs.
Several forces push in the same direction, and knowing them makes the trap easier to spot.
The first is that we hate waste.
Most of us were raised to finish what's on the plate and not to throw things out.
That's usually a good instinct.
But the sunk cost trap hijacks it.
Walking away from a bad investment feels like wasting it, even though the waste has already happened.
Staying doesn't un-waste the money.
It just adds more time or money on top.
The second reason is that losses hurt more than gains feel good.
Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky, two of the most influential researchers in this field, showed that losing $100 tends to feel roughly twice as bad as winning $100 feels good.
As long as you keep going, the loss stays open, and there's still a chance it might turn around.
The moment you stop, the loss becomes real and final.
So we keep going, hoping to avoid ever having to feel it.
The third reason is about pride.
In 1976, the organisational psychologist Barry Staw ran a study with business students.
Each student played a company executive deciding how to split research money between two divisions of a company.
Then they learned how their choice had turned out.
When the division they'd backed had done badly, students who had made that original call themselves went on to pour more money into it than students who had inherited the decision from someone else.
Staw called this escalation of commitment.
Pulling out would have meant admitting the first decision was a mistake.
Putting in more money kept that admission at bay.
You can see all three forces in ordinary life.
Someone stays in a course they no longer want to finish because they've done two years of it.
A couple keeps pouring money into a renovation that has blown out, rather than stopping and rethinking.
A person on hold with a call centre for forty minutes refuses to hang up, even though calling back tomorrow morning would be quicker.
In each case, the past is doing the deciding.
It's worth being fair here.
Not every decision to keep going is a sunk cost mistake.
Sometimes what you've already put in has genuinely changed the future.
Two years of study might mean you're only one semester from a qualification that's worth having.
The question is whether you're staying for what lies ahead, or for what's behind you.
In the final part, we'll look at some practical ways to tell the difference.
Part three. The clean slate question.
One of the best escapes from the sunk cost trap comes from a story told by Andy Grove, the long-time leader of the computer chip maker Intel.
In 1985, Intel was losing badly in the memory chip business it had been built on.
Grove and his colleague Gordon Moore had been agonising over it for months.
In his book Only the Paranoid Survive, Grove describes asking Moore a simple question.
To paraphrase it, if the board kicked us out and brought in a new chief executive, what would that person do?
Moore answered straight away that the new boss would get out of memory chips.
So Grove suggested, in effect, that they walk out the door, come back in, and do it themselves.
They did, and Intel went on to focus on the microprocessors that powered a generation of personal computers.
That's the clean slate question, and you can use it on anything.
If I were starting fresh today, knowing what I know now, would I choose this?
Would I buy this ticket tonight?
Would I enrol in this course?
Would I buy this car at this price?
If the honest answer is no, then what you've already spent is the only thing keeping you there.
A second tool is to decide your exit point in advance.
Before you start something uncertain, choose the point at which you'd stop.
For a renovation, that might be a total budget you won't go past without a proper rethink.
For a new business idea, it might be a date by which you need to see a certain number of paying customers.
For a film, it might be the half-hour mark.
It's much easier to walk away when your calmer, earlier self has already given you permission.
A third tool is to borrow some distance.
Staw's study showed that people who didn't make the original decision were better at letting it go.
So ask someone who wasn't part of the first choice.
Or imagine a friend describing your exact situation to you.
It's often obvious what they should do, even when it isn't obvious for you.
And finally, change the words you use.
Instead of saying, I'd be wasting what I spent, try saying, that money is already gone.
It sounds harsh, but it's freeing.
The money was spent the moment you paid it.
The only decision left is what to do with the next hour, the next dollar, or the next year.
Let's recap.
A sunk cost is anything you've already spent and can't recover, and the trap is letting it drive decisions that should depend only on the future.
We fall for it because we hate waste, because losses sting, and because stopping means admitting a mistake.
To escape, ask the clean slate question, set your exit point in advance, and get an outside view.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. In the theatre ticket study, who went to more plays early in the season?
Answer. The people who paid full price, rather than those given a discount.
Question two. What did Barry Staw call our tendency to keep investing in a failing decision we made ourselves?
Answer. Escalation of commitment.
Question three. What's the clean slate question?
Answer. If I were starting fresh today, knowing what I know now, would I choose this?
That's the end of The Sunk Cost Trap. See you in the next one.
